claims.explanation: Vinorelbine is a tubulin-polymerization inhibitor, so selectivity is most plausibly driven by the cellular context that determines dependence on microtubule dynamics and drug efflux/response. The strongest mechanistic candidates are high expression of the beta-tubulin isotype TUBB3 (and related TUBB/TUBA isotypes), which can alter drug binding and microtubule stability, and loss of the mitotic checkpoint/tumor-suppressor gene TP53, which permits mitotic slippage and reduces drug-induced apoptosis. Multidrug-resistance efflux via ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein) is a well-established protective mechanism for vinca alkaloids and would predict resistance in lines with high ABCB1 expression.

features.basis: Beta-III tubulin isotype alters vinca-alkaloid binding and microtubule dynamics, a known resistance mechanism
P-glycoprotein efflux of vinca alkaloids is a canonical multidrug-resistance mechanism
Loss of p53 permits mitotic slippage and reduces apoptosis after microtubule poisoning
Altered beta-tubulin isotype composition can reduce vinorelbine binding/stability
Alpha-tubulin isotype changes can modulate microtubule drug sensitivity
Microtubule-associated protein expression can influence microtubule stability and drug response
Stathmin promotes microtubule destabilization and can counteract tubulin inhibitors
Survivin overexpression supports mitotic progression and apoptosis resistance
p21 induction after microtubule inhibition can promote cell-cycle arrest rather than death
EGFR-mutant NSCLC trials show vinorelbine-based chemotherapy is less effective than EGFR TKI in this genotype
BRCA-mutant breast cancers were treated with vinorelbine as standard therapy in PARP-inhibitor trials, suggesting some sensitivity
